source_refs.note: Chapter 21 exercise (PDF 85-87), solved: 10 MCQs keyed (no key is printed), 9 short-answer, 5 constructed-response and 4 descriptive questions with model answers. MCQ II carries a Book correction.

blocks.prompt: I) Which of the following compound is a primary halogenoalkane?
blocks.explanation: In 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–Br, the C carrying Br is attached to only one other carbon, so it is primary. 2-bromo-3-methylbutane and 2-bromopropane are secondary (C–Br carbon joined to two carbons); 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary (three carbons).

blocks.prompt: II) The reactivity order of halogenoalkanes for a particular alkyl group is:
blocks.explanation: Reactivity is decided by the C–X bond strength: C–I 228 < C–Br 290 < C–Cl 346 < C–F 467 kJ mol⁻¹. The weakest bond breaks most easily, so R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (b) is misprinted: it names Chloride twice and leaves out Iodide (“Chloride > Bromide > Fluoride > Chloride”). It is a wrong option either way; the key (c) is not affected.

blocks.prompt: III) SN2 reactions can be best carried out with:
blocks.explanation: In primary halogenoalkanes the carbon bearing X is attached to H atoms or only one carbon, so there is little steric hindrance and the nucleophile can attack easily from the back side. Primary halogenoalkanes always follow SN2.

blocks.prompt: IV) Elimination bimolecular reactions involve:
blocks.explanation: E2: Rate = k [Alkyl halide]¹[Base]¹, order = 1 + 1 = 2, so second order kinetics.

blocks.prompt: V) For which mechanisms, the first step involved is the same:
blocks.explanation: In both SN1 and E1 the first (slow, rate-determining) step is the ionization of the alkyl halide to a carbocation and X⁻. Then a nucleophile attacks the carbocation (SN1) or a base removes a β-H (E1). E2 and SN2 are single-step.

blocks.prompt: VI) Halogenoalkanes are considered to be very reactive compounds towards nucleophiles, because:

options.text: They have an electrophilic carbon and a good leaving group
They have an electrophilic carbon and a bad leaving group
They have a nucleophilic carbon and a good leaving group

blocks.explanation: The polar C–X bond gives the carbon a partial positive charge (electrophilic carbon) that attracts nucleophiles, and the halide ion leaves easily (good leaving group), so substitution takes place readily.

blocks.prompt: VII) 2-chloropropane will follow which mechanism when it reacts with aqueous KOH resulting in the formation of an alcohol.
blocks.explanation: 2-chloropropane, CH₃–CHCl–CH₃, is a secondary halogenoalkane. Secondary halogenoalkanes can react by both SN2 and SN1, depending on the solvent, so the alcohol (propan-2-ol) forms by a mixed SN1 and SN2 mechanism. E1 gives an alkene, not an alcohol.

blocks.prompt: VIII) Which one of the following is not a nucleophile?
blocks.explanation: A nucleophile has a lone pair (or negative charge) to donate. H₂O, H₂S and NH₃ have lone pairs. BF₃ has no lone pair on B; boron is electron deficient (6 electrons), so BF₃ accepts electrons: it is an electrophile (Lewis acid).

blocks.prompt: IX) When aqueous solution of alkyl halides are reacted with AgNO₃, the most rapid ppt. formation occurs with:
blocks.explanation: C–I is the weakest bond (228 kJ mol⁻¹), so an iodoalkane is hydrolysed fastest and releases I⁻ quickest; Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI (bright yellow ppt) appears first. A chloroalkane reacts very slowly.

blocks.prompt: X) The rate of E1 reaction depends upon:

options.text: The concentrations of substrate as well as base
Neither the concentration of substrate nor the base

blocks.explanation: E1 is unimolecular: only the alkyl halide takes part in the slow ionization step, so Rate = k [Alkyl halide]; the base is not involved in the rate-determining step.

blocks.prompt: a) Why halogenoalkanes are known to be very reactive compounds?
blocks.explanation: Because of the electronegativity difference, the C–X bond is polar: carbon carries δ+ and becomes an electrophilic centre that nucleophiles attack, and X⁻ is a good leaving group. A base can also remove the β-hydrogen. So they readily give nucleophilic substitution and elimination reactions.

blocks.prompt: b) Why fluoroalkanes rarely undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions?
blocks.explanation: The C–F bond is the strongest carbon–halogen bond (467 kJ mol⁻¹, against C–Cl 346, C–Br 290, C–I 228). It is so strong that it is not broken under ordinary conditions, so fluoroalkanes are the least reactive halogenoalkanes.

blocks.prompt: c) Why primary halogenoalkanes undergo substitution reactions by SN2 mechanism?
blocks.explanation: In a primary halogenoalkane the carbon bearing X is attached to H atoms or only one carbon (little steric hindrance), so the nucleophile can easily attack it from the side opposite the leaving group in one step. A primary carbocation is the least stable, so the SN1 route is not favoured.

blocks.prompt: d) Does 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane undergo elimination reaction or not? Justify.
blocks.explanation: No. Its structure is (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–Br. β-elimination needs a hydrogen on the β-carbon (the carbon next to C–Br). Here the β-carbon is bonded to three CH₃ groups and the CH₂Br group and carries no hydrogen, so HBr cannot be removed and no alkene forms.

blocks.prompt: e) Why tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo elimination reaction by E1 mechanism?
blocks.explanation: A tertiary halogenoalkane ionizes easily to a tertiary carbocation, which is the most stable carbocation (+I effect of three alkyl groups). The three bulky groups also block a one-step attack. So the slow first step forms the carbocation, then a base removes a β-H to give the alkene: the E1 route.

blocks.prompt: f) Hydroxide ion is a good base as well as a good nucleophile. Justify.
blocks.explanation: OH⁻ has a negative charge and lone pairs. As a nucleophile it attacks the electrophilic carbon and replaces X: C₂H₅Br + NaOH(aq) → C₂H₅OH + NaBr. As a base it removes the β-hydrogen: C₂H₅Br + NaOH (alcohol) → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + NaBr. So bromoethane gives both ethanol and ethene.

blocks.prompt: g) What is the role of iron chloride (FeCl₃) during the chlorination of benzene?
blocks.explanation: Anhydrous FeCl₃ is the catalyst for this electrophilic aromatic substitution at room temperature: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → (FeCl₃) C₆H₅Cl + HCl. As a Lewis acid it polarises Cl₂ and gives the electrophile Cl⁺ (Cl₂ + FeCl₃ → Cl⁺ + FeCl₄⁻) that attacks the ring (the Cl⁺ step is beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: h) Which among haloalkanes or haloarenes, is more reactive towards nucleophiles?
blocks.explanation: Haloalkanes are more reactive. In haloarenes the lone pair of the halogen is delocalised into the benzene ring, giving the C–X bond partial double-bond character; the bond becomes stronger and hard to break, so haloarenes are much less reactive towards nucleophiles.

blocks.prompt: i) Write the equation for the reaction of 1-chloropropane with AgNO₃.
blocks.explanation:
In water–ethanol, water replaces Cl, and the Cl⁻ released gives a white precipitate (slowly):
CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + H₂O → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + H⁺ + Cl⁻
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl (white ppt)
Overall: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + AgNO₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + AgCl↓ + HNO₃

blocks.prompt: a) Predict the mechanism which the chloroalkane will adopt while giving nucleophilic substitution reactions.
blocks.explanation:
It depends on the type of chloroalkane:
• Primary (e.g. CH₃CH₂Cl): SN2. Little steric hindrance, nucleophile attacks from the back in one step; Rate = k [RCl][Nu⁻].
• Tertiary (e.g. (CH₃)₃CCl): SN1. Forms a stable tertiary carbocation; bulky groups block back-side attack; Rate = k [RCl].
• Secondary (e.g. CH₃CHClCH₃): SN1 or SN2 (mixed), depending on the solvent.

blocks.prompt: b) Why nucleophilic substitution and elimination reactions of haloalkanes proceed together under similar conditions?
blocks.explanation: The same reagent (e.g. OH⁻) is both a nucleophile and a base. In a haloalkane the δ+ carbon can be attacked by it as a nucleophile (substitution → alcohol), while the β-hydrogen can be removed by it as a base (elimination → alkene). Both sites are present in one molecule, so the two reactions compete; e.g. bromoethane with NaOH gives ethanol and ethene. Conditions decide the main product: aqueous NaOH favours substitution, NaOH in alcohol favours elimination.

blocks.prompt: c) It is difficult for chlorobenzene to undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions but it is easier for it to undergo electrophilic substitution reactions. Give reasons.
blocks.explanation:
Nucleophilic substitution is difficult: the lone pair of Cl is delocalised into the ring, so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and is strong; it does not break under normal conditions (no reaction with NaOH). Also the electron-rich ring repels an attacking nucleophile.
Electrophilic substitution is easier: the benzene ring has a cloud of delocalised π electrons that attracts electrophiles, and the Cl lone pair pushed into the ring adds electron density. Substitution keeps the stable aromatic ring, so electrophiles (Cl⁺, NO₂⁺ etc.) replace a ring H (the electrophilic part is beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: d) Differentiate between E2 and E1 reactions. Draw a table for your response.
blocks.explanation: Both remove HX to give an alkene; they differ in the number of steps and in what controls the rate.

rows: One step: base removes β-H and X⁻ leaves at the same time
Two steps: slow ionization, then base removes β-H
Two molecules in the rate-determining step
One molecule in the rate-determining step

blocks.prompt: e) Why does CH₃-CH₂-I give a precipitate with aqueous silver nitrate earlier than CH₃-CH₂-Cl?
blocks.explanation: The C–I bond (228 kJ mol⁻¹) is much weaker than C–Cl (346 kJ mol⁻¹), so iodoethane is hydrolysed faster and releases I⁻ quickly: Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI (bright yellow ppt) appears at once. Chloroethane releases Cl⁻ very slowly, so the white AgCl ppt forms late.

blocks.prompt:
Q4. Describe how substitution of alcohol with following reagents help to synthesize halogenoalkanes
i) KBr with H₂SO₄  ii) SOCl₂/Pyridine  iii) PCl₃  iv) PCl₅
blocks.explanation:
In each case the –OH group of the alcohol is replaced by a halogen atom.
i) KBr with H₂SO₄: the acid reacts with KBr to give HBr, which then converts the alcohol into a bromoalkane.
CH₃–CH₂–OH + KBr + H₂SO₄ → CH₃–CH₂–Br + H₂O + KHSO₄
This method is used for bromoalkanes and iodoalkanes; H₃PO₄ is preferred for iodoalkanes because it is a weak oxidizing agent and does not oxidize I⁻ to I₂.
ii) SOCl₂/pyridine: thionyl chloride with pyridine as catalyst gives the chloroalkane.
CH₃–CH₂–OH + SOCl₂ → (pyridine) CH₃–CH₂–Cl + SO₂ + HCl
The by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases and escape, leaving the pure product; so this is the best method.
iii) PCl₃: phosphorus trichloride replaces three –OH groups.
3CH₃–CH₂–OH + PCl₃ → 3CH₃–CH₂–Cl + H₃PO₃
(The book prints this reaction with PBr₃: 3CH₃CH₂OH + PBr₃ → 3CH₃CH₂Br + H₃PO₃.)
iv) PCl₅: phosphorus pentachloride.
CH₃–CH₂–OH + PCl₅ → CH₃–CH₂–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl
(Alcohols also give chloroalkanes with HCl and ZnCl₂ catalyst: CH₃CH₂OH + HCl → (ZnCl₂) CH₃CH₂Cl + H₂O.)

blocks.prompt:
Q5. Describe nucleophilic substitution reactions of halogenoalkane starting from bromoethane with following reagents:
i) Aqueous NaOH  ii) Ethanolic KCN  iii) Ethanolic NH₃
blocks.explanation:
In each reaction the nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon of CH₃–CH₂–Br and Br⁻ leaves.
i) Aqueous NaOH: OH⁻ is a good nucleophile; heating under reflux (to avoid loss of volatile products) gives ethanol.
CH₃–CH₂–Br + NaOH(aq) → CH₃–CH₂–OH + NaBr
Because OH⁻ is also a good base, some elimination also occurs (in alcohol it gives ethene): CH₃–CH₂–Br + NaOH (alcohol) → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + NaBr.
ii) Ethanolic KCN: CN⁻ is a strong nucleophile but a weak base, so only substitution occurs. Bromoethane is heated with ethanolic KCN under reflux to give propanenitrile (the carbon chain grows by one C).
CH₃–CH₂–Br + KCN → (alcohol) CH₃–CH₂–C≡N + KBr
iii) Ethanolic NH₃: the lone pair of N attacks the carbon; ethanamine is formed.
CH₃–CH₂–Br + NH₃ → CH₃–CH₂–NH₂ + HBr
Ethanamine is also a nucleophile and reacts further:
C₂H₅NH₂ + C₂H₅Br → (C₂H₅)₂NH (N-ethylethanamine) + HBr
(C₂H₅)₂NH + C₂H₅Br → (C₂H₅)₃N (N,N-diethylethanamine) + HBr
With a large excess of bromoethane the quaternary ammonium salt forms:
(C₂H₅)₃N + C₂H₅Br → [(C₂H₅)₄N]⁺Br⁻
By controlling the amounts of bromoethane and ammonia the required amine is obtained (excess NH₃ gives mainly ethanamine).

blocks.prompt: Q6. Compare the reactivity of halogenoalkanes and halogenoarenes using chloroethane and chlorobenzene as examples.
blocks.explanation: In chloroethane the C–Cl bond is polar; the δ+ carbon is attacked by nucleophiles and the β-H by bases, so it gives substitution and elimination easily (e.g. CH₃CH₂Cl + NaOH(aq) → CH₃CH₂OH + NaCl). In chlorobenzene the lone pair of Cl is delocalised into the benzene ring; the C–Cl bond gets partial double-bond character, becomes stronger and is difficult to break. So chlorobenzene does not react with NaOH under normal conditions, does not undergo elimination, and is less reactive and synthetically less useful.

rows: Cl is attached to an sp³ alkyl carbon
Cl is attached to a carbon of the benzene ring
Lone pair of Cl stays on Cl
Lone pair of Cl is delocalised into the ring
C–Cl is a pure single bond
C–Cl bond is weaker, easily broken
C–Cl bond is stronger, difficult to break
Reacts with aqueous NaOH → ethanol (and ethene)
Does not react with NaOH under normal conditions
Gives elimination with a base → ethene

blocks.prompt: Q7. Describe the SN1 and SN2 mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution in halogenoalkanes.
blocks.explanation:
Nucleophilic substitution involves two processes: breaking of the C–X bond (departure of the leaving group) and formation of the C–Nu bond (attack of the nucleophile). If both happen together in one step the mechanism is SN2; if the bond breaks first and the new bond forms in a second step, it is SN1.
SN2 (nucleophilic substitution bimolecular), e.g. bromomethane + OH⁻:
1. OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of CH₃–Br from the side opposite to Br.
2. As the C–O bond starts forming, the C–Br bond starts breaking (bond formation = bond breaking). A transition state [HO···CH₃···Br]⁻ forms, with carbon partly bonded to both OH and Br.
3. Br⁻ leaves and methanol forms; the three H atoms flip to the other side.
CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻
One step, which is the rate-determining step, with two molecules in it: Rate = k [Alkyl halide]¹[Nucleophile]¹, order 2. Primary halogenoalkanes always follow SN2 (little steric hindrance).
SN1 (nucleophilic substitution unimolecular), e.g. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane + OH⁻ (in aqueous acetone or aqueous ethanol):
Step 1 (slow): reversible ionization: (CH₃)₃C–Br ⇌ (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻ (a planar tertiary carbocation).
Step 2 (fast): OH⁻ attacks the carbocation: (CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃C–OH.
Step 1 breaks a covalent bond, so it is slow and rate-determining; only one molecule takes part: Rate = k [Alkyl halide], first order. Tertiary halogenoalkanes always follow SN1 because the tertiary carbocation is the most stable (+I effect; stability 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl) and the three bulky groups block back-side attack. Secondary halogenoalkanes can follow both, depending on the solvent.

rows: No intermediate; a transition state HO···C···Br
Bond breaking first, bond making later
Bond breaking and bond making at the same time
